strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and ambitious imaging problem: reconstructing 31-channel hyperspectral images from a same-resolution grayscale measurement captured through a single phase-only diffractive/metalens optic. The minimalist filterless setup is well motivated for compact, light-efficient snapshot HSI, and the work has clear relevance to computational photography and computational imaging.

The proposed method is technically coherent: patch-based conditional diffusion is paired with full-field PSF-based guidance to resolve cross-patch ambiguity caused by the optical blur. The least-squares patch rescaling and measurement-consistency guidance are sensible design choices, and the ablations show that both guidance and rescaling materially improve performance.

The empirical evaluation is fairly extensive for a simulation paper. The authors compare against several recent HSI reconstruction baselines, report SAM/SSIM/PSNR, include visual spectral profiles, evaluate multiple optical PSF designs, provide ablations over patch size/stride/guidance, discuss runtime, and test cross-dataset/high-resolution generalization on CAVE, ICVL, and Harvard.

The uncertainty estimation is a valuable byproduct of the diffusion formulation. The reported correlation between sampled uncertainty and reconstruction error is compelling and useful for real deployments where spectral estimates may be trusted unevenly across the scene.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. The optical model, diffusion formulation, sampling procedure, and supplementary implementation details are described in enough detail to make the approach understandable and likely reproducible, assuming the promised code is released.
weaknesses: The central limitation is that all main evidence is simulation-based. For a paper whose motivation is a new physical imaging architecture, the absence of any real captured measurements or prototype validation leaves uncertainty about robustness to real optical aberrations, calibration errors, sensor nonidealities, diffraction efficiency variation, stray light, fabrication tolerances, demosaicing, exposure, dynamic range, and non-Gaussian noise.

The physical assumptions are somewhat idealized. The paper assumes a shift-invariant wavelength-dependent PSF and known forward model, but real metalens systems may exhibit field-dependent PSFs, polarization effects, manufacturing deviations, chromatic efficiency variations, and calibration drift. The supplementary noise study helps, but additive Gaussian noise is only a partial stress test.

The comparison to baselines is useful but not fully definitive. Many baselines were designed for different sensing models and full-field fixed-resolution processing, whereas the proposed model is tailored to the PSF-guided patch setting. It is unclear whether stronger physics-informed adaptations of transformer/unfolding methods, or diffusion baselines with full-field conditioning, would narrow the gap.

The method is computationally heavy at inference when guidance is used. The reported 20-guidance-iteration setting takes on the order of tens of seconds for 256x256 reconstruction on an RTX 3090, and high-resolution use will be dominated by repeated guidance convolutions. This is acceptable for some scientific settings but weakens claims toward practical snapshot imaging unless speedups are developed.

Some claims are phrased quite strongly, such as demonstrating that local optical cues are sufficient to capture full spectral information. The results support that local cues plus a learned natural-image prior and global forward-model guidance can work well in simulation, but they do not prove sufficiency in a broader physical or distributional sense.

The RGB/Bayer discussion is slightly confusing because the supplement notes that the main-paper three-channel results effectively assume uniform filters rather than true Bayer mosaicing. This should be made more prominent in the main text to avoid overstating the realism of the Bayer comparisons.

strengths: The paper studies an interesting and potentially impactful minimalist hyperspectral imaging setting: reconstructing a 31-channel HSI from a single filterless grayscale measurement produced by a phase-only diffractive optic. If validated, this could be valuable for compact snapshot spectral imaging.

The proposed patch-based conditional diffusion model with global PSF-based guidance is technically sensible and well motivated for scaling to larger resolutions. The paper includes useful ablations for guidance, patch size, patch rescaling, overlap, and number of guidance iterations.

The simulation results on ARAD1K show clear gains over several adapted hyperspectral reconstruction baselines in the proposed filterless+optic setting, and the cross-dataset experiments on ICVL, Harvard, and CAVE provide some evidence that the learned patch prior is not purely memorizing the training distribution.

The paper is generally clear, with equations, pseudocode, runtime measurements, optical-design details, and a discussion of uncertainty estimation. The uncertainty-error correlation experiment is a useful addition.
weaknesses: The central imaging claim is not convincingly supported because all main evidence is simulation-based. There is no real optical prototype, no captured measurements, no calibration experiment, and no validation under real sensor effects, fabrication errors, field-dependent PSFs, depth variation, lens misalignment, spectral response uncertainty, vignetting, or photon/shot noise. For a paper whose motivation is a new class of physical hyperspectral cameras, this is a major gap.

The optical model is highly idealized: the forward model assumes a known shift-invariant PSF and far-field scene radiance mapped by an ideal lens. Real flat optics are typically field-, wavelength-, polarization-, and fabrication-sensitive. The paper does not show that the simulated PSFs can be manufactured with the claimed performance or that reconstruction remains stable under plausible PSF mismatch.

The comparisons are not fully satisfying. The baselines are mostly architectures developed for different measurement models, then minimally adapted. The paper does not compare against strong physics-based or plug-and-play inverse solvers using the same known forward model, nor against methods specifically tuned for this new grayscale diffractive setup. This weakens the claim that the proposed approach is uniquely capable.

The reported gains depend heavily on test-time guidance and per-patch least-squares rescaling. This makes the method slower than the headline patch model suggests and leaves radiometric fidelity somewhat unclear. Runtime is substantial for 256x256 reconstruction at the chosen settings, and scaling to megapixel images may be dominated by repeated full-field convolutions.

The Bayer/RGB results are somewhat misleading: the supplement states that the main results effectively assume three sequential uniformly filtered captures rather than a true Bayer mosaic with demosaicing. This should be much clearer in the main text, since it changes the acquisition assumptions.

The experimental evidence is narrow relative to the strength of the claims. The main quantitative test set is only 50 ARAD1K images, cross-dataset evaluation uses small samples, and noise robustness is only synthetic Gaussian noise. There is little analysis of failure cases beyond uncertainty visualizations.

The lens design study appears partly hand-tuned and empirical. The paper identifies good PSFs but does not provide a principled optical optimization objective tied to reconstruction performance, nor does it quantify manufacturing feasibility, throughput across wavelengths, or sensitivity to optical perturbations.

The paper sometimes overstates its contribution, e.g. claiming the first high-quality demonstration of grayscale chromatic-aberration hyperspectral reconstruction, while the demonstration is entirely simulated and depends on ideal knowledge of the PSF. A more careful framing as a simulation study would be more scientifically convincing.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and difficult computational imaging setting: reconstructing a 31-channel HSI from a single filterless grayscale measurement with the same spatial pixel count, using only chromatic aberration from a phase-only/flat optic. This is a meaningful and original problem formulation with clear relevance to compact snapshot hyperspectral imaging.

The proposed combination of patch-based conditional diffusion with PSF-based global guidance is technically well motivated. The guidance mechanism directly addresses the ambiguity introduced by processing blurred measurements in small patches, and the scale correction is a practical solution to the patch-normalization ambiguity.

The empirical evidence is strong for a simulated Algorithms/General contribution: the method outperforms multiple retrained HSI reconstruction baselines on ARAD1K in the filterless+optic setting, with sizeable gains in PSNR, SSIM, and SAM. The ablations convincingly show the value of guidance, patch rescaling, patch size, and overlapping patches.

The paper goes beyond a single benchmark comparison by studying different PSF/lens designs, uncertainty estimates, cross-dataset high-resolution generalization, and measurement-noise robustness in the supplement. These analyses make the scientific case more complete than a standard benchmark-only paper.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. The image formation model, diffusion formulation, sampling algorithm, and optical design discussion are understandable, and the supplement provides useful implementation details such as model configuration, runtime, metrics, and PSF design theory.
weaknesses: The central experimental limitation is that the work is entirely simulation-based. The claims about enabling a new class of real high-resolution, light-efficient cameras are plausible but not fully demonstrated without a physical prototype, real sensor noise, calibration error, manufacturing tolerances, wavelength-dependent efficiency variation, and real optical misalignment effects.

The method assumes an accurate known PSF and forward model at inference. In practice, PSF mismatch, field dependence, finite depth, non-Lambertian effects, sensor nonlinearities, and calibration drift could materially affect performance; these are not stress-tested beyond a simple additive Gaussian noise model.

The comparison to prior methods is useful but not definitive. Many baselines were designed for different optical encodings and fixed-resolution full-field reconstruction, while the proposed method is tailored to this PSF-guided patch setting. The paper would be stronger with comparisons to inverse-problem diffusion/posterior sampling methods using the same forward model and with stronger optimization-based or plug-and-play baselines.

Runtime is nontrivial: the reported default uses 20 DDIM steps and 20 guidance iterations, with accuracy improving further at higher guidance counts. This may be acceptable for offline reconstruction, but the paper could better discuss throughput, memory scaling, and practicality for high-resolution deployment.

The uncertainty analysis is promising but incomplete. A Pearson correlation of 0.80 with reconstruction error is useful, yet it does not establish calibration, coverage, or decision-theoretic reliability of the uncertainty estimates.

Some claims are phrased strongly, such as being the first high-quality reconstruction solely from grayscale chromatic aberration and local optical cues being sufficient for full spectral information. The presented evidence supports these claims within the simulated datasets and lens models, but the wording should be tempered to reflect the simulated setting and the dependence on learned natural-image priors.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and underexplored computational imaging setting: reconstructing a 31-channel HSI from a single filterless grayscale measurement captured through one diffractive/flat optic. This is a meaningful vision/imaging contribution even though the setting is intrinsically ill-posed.

The proposed guided patch diffusion approach is technically well motivated. Training on small patches addresses limited HSI data, while inference-time physical guidance enforces global measurement consistency and directly addresses cross-patch ambiguity from a large PSF.

The experimental evidence is broad: ARAD1K simulation against multiple adapted HSI reconstruction baselines, ablations on guidance, patch size, rescaling, overlap, PSF designs, noise robustness, cross-dataset tests on ICVL/Harvard/CAVE, and additional CASSI experiments in the supplement.

The work includes a real fabricated metalens prototype and tabletop reconstructions, not only simulation. The calibration, PSF measurement, shift-invariance checks, LoRA sim-to-real adaptation, and per-scene metrics make the systems claim considerably more convincing.

The method provides uncertainty estimates via diffusion sampling, and the paper evaluates their relation to reconstruction error in both simulation and experiment. This is practically useful for such an ill-posed inverse problem.

The manuscript is clear and unusually complete: limitations are explicitly discussed, implementation/training details are provided, and the supplementary material substantially improves reproducibility and interpretability.
weaknesses: The real-world validation is still modest: only 8 experimental test scenes after finetuning on 6 tabletop scenes from the same overall capture setup. This supports feasibility but does not fully establish robustness to broader scenes, depths, lighting, materials, or field conditions.

The reconstruction depends fundamentally on local spatial texture at the PSF scale; homogeneous regions are provably ambiguous and empirically weak. This is honestly acknowledged, but it significantly limits the applicability of a filterless design for common scenes with smooth surfaces or large uniform objects.

Inference is computationally expensive. Reported runtimes range from tens of seconds at 256x256 to 13 minutes for the experimental crop and up to 52 minutes for high-resolution datasets, making the method unsuitable for many practical snapshot-imaging workflows without future acceleration.

The baseline comparison is reasonable but not definitive because most competing models were designed for better-conditioned CASSI or RGB/Bayer settings rather than this filterless optical model. The paper adapts them, but stronger comparisons to optimization-based physical reconstruction, plug-and-play priors, or specifically tuned diffusion/posterior sampling baselines would further strengthen the case.

The optical design study is empirical and somewhat hand-tuned. The paper compares several PSFs and finds R1/T4 work well, but it does not optimize the optic jointly with the reconstruction model or provide a principled design criterion, so the optical conclusions are suggestive rather than complete.

The uncertainty analysis demonstrates correlation with error, but not full probabilistic calibration, coverage, or decision-theoretic usefulness. The claim that the samples represent reliable posterior uncertainty should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

The experimental pipeline relies on calibrated PSFs, spectral scaling from paired calibration scenes, and LoRA finetuning with imperfectly registered reference HSIs. These are reasonable for a prototype, but the amount of calibration required reduces the immediacy of the claimed hardware simplicity.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and underexplored imaging setting: reconstructing a 31-channel HSI from a single filterless grayscale snapshot captured through one flat optic. The combination of a patch diffusion prior with global PSF-consistency guidance is technically plausible and well motivated for the large-kernel patch ambiguity the authors identify.

The manuscript is generally clear and includes useful ablations: guidance vs. no guidance, patch size, overlapping patches, patch rescaling, PSF/lens design, noise robustness, and uncertainty/error correlation. These experiments make the method easier to interpret than a purely black-box reconstruction system.

The work includes a fabricated metalens prototype and real tabletop captures, not only simulation. The experimental section gives calibration details, reports real-scene metrics, and acknowledges important limitations such as failure on homogeneous regions and high reconstruction cost.

The uncertainty estimates are a useful secondary output. The reported correlations with reconstruction error in both simulation and experiment are promising, and this is a meaningful practical advantage over deterministic baselines.
weaknesses: The central scientific claim remains only partially convincing because the strongest results are simulated using known forward models and datasets of natural scenes. The real validation is narrow: 15 tabletop scenes total, six used for finetuning, eight for testing, with no shared objects but still a highly constrained indoor domain. This is not enough to establish broad practical viability of filterless HSI reconstruction.

The real experiment depends on several fragile calibration and adaptation steps: adjacent reference camera capture, approximate homography registration, spectral scaling from calibration scenes, simulated pretraining with measured PSF, and LoRA finetuning on a few real scenes. These steps make it difficult to isolate how much performance comes from the proposed optical encoding versus domain-specific learning and calibration.

The baseline comparison is not fully satisfying. The main baselines are methods designed for related but better-conditioned HSI settings, modified to this unusual measurement model. This is understandable, but it weakens the conclusion that the proposed method is broadly superior; poor baseline adaptation or insufficient tuning could explain some of the gap. There is also no strong real-hardware baseline, such as alternative reconstruction algorithms on the prototype data.

The method is computationally heavy: 22 seconds for 256x256 simulation, 13 minutes for real 640x960 crops, and up to 52 minutes for high-resolution cross-dataset cases. This substantially limits the impact for many snapshot-imaging applications, and acceleration is mostly discussed speculatively via distillation rather than demonstrated.

The ill-posedness is severe, and the paper’s own limitation analysis shows that homogeneous regions are fundamentally problematic. This is not a minor corner case for hyperspectral imaging, where many materials or calibration targets can be spatially smooth. The method may be recovering plausible natural-scene spectra rather than reliably measuring spectra in many practically important cases.

The experimental evaluation of uncertainty is encouraging but not yet decisive. Correlation with error is reported, but there is limited calibration analysis of the probabilistic predictions, limited discussion of failure cases where uncertainty is overconfident, and no downstream decision-making experiment showing practical value.

Reproducibility is uncertain from the manuscript alone. The method relies on custom optics, measured PSFs, calibration procedures, a 75M-parameter diffusion model, and extensive training/inference details; without released code, trained models, PSFs, and raw calibration data, independent verification would be difficult.

Overall, while the paper has real merits, I do not find the evidence strong enough for acceptance. The contribution is intriguing, but the practical and scientific claims are overextended relative to the limited real-world validation and the dependence on calibration, priors, and slow guided sampling.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored computational imaging setting: reconstructing a full hyperspectral cube from a single filterless grayscale snapshot captured through one flat diffractive optic. This is a compelling applied/systems contribution with clear relevance to compact, high-throughput hyperspectral cameras.

The core method is well motivated. Patch-based diffusion is a sensible response to scarce HSI training data, and the proposed PSF-based global guidance directly addresses the otherwise severe cross-patch ambiguity caused by wavelength-dependent blur. The scale-recovery step for patch-normalized predictions is also a practical and thoughtful component.

The empirical evidence is broad and convincing. The paper reports strong simulated performance on ARAD1K, cross-dataset tests on ICVL/Harvard/CAVE, comparisons across multiple PSF designs, ablations for guidance, patch size, overlap, and scaling, and additional CASSI experiments showing that the framework is not limited to the main filterless setup.

The experimental prototype substantially strengthens the paper. Fabricating and calibrating an R1 metalens, measuring PSFs, finetuning on real paired captures, and evaluating on held-out tabletop scenes make the claim more credible than a simulation-only computational imaging paper.

The uncertainty analysis is a valuable secondary contribution. Sampling-based uncertainty correlates well with true error in both simulation and experiment, which is especially useful for such an ill-posed reconstruction problem.
The manuscript is clearly written and unusually candid about limitations, including texture dependence, homogeneous-region failures, lack of global context propagation, and high reconstruction cost.
weaknesses: The experimental validation, while impressive, remains limited in scale: only 15 captured tabletop scenes are used, with 6 for finetuning and 8 for testing. This is enough for a proof of concept, but not enough to fully establish robustness across realistic scenes, depths, lighting conditions, materials, or outdoor settings.

The method is computationally expensive. Reported reconstruction time is about 22 seconds for 256x256 simulation, 13 minutes for experimental 640x960 crops, and up to 52 minutes for high-resolution Harvard/ICVL scenes. This weakens the practical deployment case unless offline reconstruction is acceptable.

The comparison to prior methods is reasonable but imperfect because most baselines were designed for different, better-conditioned HSI measurement models rather than this filterless single-optic setting. The paper adapts them carefully, but the performance gap partly reflects a new problem formulation where baselines are not specialized.

The hardware model makes several assumptions that may limit deployment, especially shift-invariant PSF behavior, truncated PSF support, approximate spectral calibration, and homography-based alignment for real supervision. The supplement addresses these, but the method’s sensitivity to calibration error and field-dependent aberrations is not fully quantified.

The approach fundamentally relies on spatial texture at the PSF scale, and homogeneous regions are unrecoverable or poorly recovered. The paper acknowledges and analyzes this failure mode, but it is a substantial limitation for many hyperspectral imaging applications involving smooth surfaces or large uniform materials.

The algorithmic novelty is more in the integration of patch diffusion, physical guidance, and flat-optic HSI reconstruction than in a wholly new diffusion formulation. The contribution is still valuable, but its originality is strongest as an applied computational imaging system rather than as a general-purpose generative modeling advance.
